new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened via its text (Hercus 1986, Victorian languages: a late survey, PL B-77). All four quoted passages are present at the stated locators, differing only by scanned letter-spacing: (1) p.115, sec. 4.2.3 'Accentuation' (Madimadi chapter), the text: 'The system of accentuation of Madimadi differed considerably from the accentuation of the other Kulin languages, which invariably had a heavy stress accent on the first syllable.' (2) p.155, Narinari note, (d) Finals (i), the text: 'In the standard Kulin languages, both eastern and western, as exemplified by Wergaia, Wembawemba and Woiwuru, a word can end in any consonant whatsoever..' and (e) Word-length and accentuation, lines 8479-8481: 'Nar…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the first syllable of the word (the general Kulin pattern Hercus reports from her own recordings); in her Woiwuru transcriptions every polysyllable carries initial primary stress, with a secondary stress on the third syllable of words of three or more syllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not stated in prose for Woiwuru; her Woiwuru transcriptions consistently mark secondary stress on the third syllable (e.g. [ˈgalpaˌninjan], [ˈdjɪrəməˌlaŋ], [ˈŋamaˌdjitj]) and on the second member of reduplications ([ˈbalamˈbalam]).
new_statements.exceptions: None for Woiwuru. Hercus notes for Kulin generally that Madimadi (and Wadiwadi) are the exception with conditioned second-syllable stress; song accentuation differs from speech.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level citation forms elicited from the last rememberers (Wandin family, Healesville, 1960s); Hercus stresses the Woiwuru material is 'so slight that only tentative remarks can be made'. The explicit prose rule is stated for the Kulin languages as a group, not in the Woiwuru section itself; the Woiwuru-specific evidence is her stress-marked phonetic transcriptions.
new_statements.identity_note: Hercus 1986 describes 'Woiwuru' = Woiwurrung proper (Wurundjeri, Yarra/Healesville-Coranderrk), i.e. the Woiwurrung dialect of Glottolog's Woiwurrung-Thagungwurrung (woiw1237); nothing first-hand exists for the Thagungwurrung (Taungurung) or Boonwurrung dialects. Her explicit prose rule is phrased for 'the Kulin languages' (eastern and western, expressly including Woiwuru, p.155); the Woiwuru-specific evidence is her stress-marked transcriptions of c. 80 words from rememberers, all with initial primary stress.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (initial stress, from Hercus 1986's Kulin-level statement); Blake 1991 gives the Woiwurrung-specific statement, framed explicitly as an assumption for a language known only from old written sources, and adds that a few words' notations suggest non-initial stress or vowel length (barrúk 'kangaroo rat').
new_statements.rule_in_words: Blake, reconstituting Woiwurrung from nineteenth-century written sources, assumes primary stress on the first syllable of the word, as in most Australian languages, and builds his vowel analysis on that assumption (three vowels in stressed syllables, schwa-like reduction in unstressed syllables); for a few words the early spellings suggest non-initial stress or a long vowel (or both), e.g. 'kangaroo rat' barrúk ~ bárruuk ~ barrúuk.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none seen in the visible text (only 'primary stress' on the first syllable is stated; the rest of p.61-62 was not visible)
new_statements.exceptions: p.62: 'The notation of a few words suggests a non-initial stress or long vowel or both', illustrated with 'kangaroo rat' (Thomas/Robinson spellings ber-uke, baroke, bar.oke, burooke, burroke) = barrúk, bárruuk or barrúuk; p.62 also says the early spellings otherwise fulfil the expectation of fewer vowel distinctions in unstressed than stressed syllables (dharrak 'arm', wang(ga) 'cheek').
new_statements.identity_note: Blake 1991 describes Woiwurrung, the Melbourne language (with Boonwurrung and Thagungwurrung material treated as the same language), reconstituted from nineteenth-century written records (Thomas, Green, Robinson, Bunce, Curr, Mathews) plus Hercus's late recordings; the stress statement is an explicit analytic assumption, not an observation from fluent speakers.

sources.note: The work says nothing about Woiwurrung or the Kulin languages. Its general claim that the prototypical Australian pattern is initial stress is compatible with the catalog's fixed: initial syllable record and with the Hercus 1986 statement, but it is not a statement about this language, so it neither confirms nor refines the catalog entry. Note the listing's parenthetical '(Miriwung = language no. 51 on the stress map)' refers to Figure 1 p. 66, an Arnhem Land/Kimberley map unrelated to Woiwurrung; it appears to be a mis-carried tag from another language's target record.
